211	type Rule = { limit: number; windowMs: number };
212	type Verdict = { allowed: boolean; retryAfterSeconds?: number };
213	
214	/** Matches LoginAttempt.scope. One table, three independent buckets. */
215	type Scope = "ip" | "account" | "signup";
216	
217	/**
218	 * One consumed attempt. `id` is the LoginAttempt primary key.
219	 *
220	 * `settledAt` is when this process last knew the row to be committed — the
221	 * moment its INSERT resolved, or, for a hit read back out of the table, the row
222	 * timestamp itself. It stays undefined while the INSERT is still queued or in
223	 * flight, and if the INSERT fails it stays undefined for good. A reconcile uses
224	 * it to tell "the read has not caught up with me yet" (keep the hit) from "the
225	 * read is authoritative and this row is gone" (drop it) — see `reconcile`.
226	 */
227	type Hit = { id: string; at: number; settledAt?: number };
228	
229	type Store = { scope: Scope; rules: Rule[]; hits: Map<string, Hit[]> };
230	
231	const MINUTE = 60_000;
232	const HOUR = 60 * MINUTE;
233	const DAY = 24 * HOUR;
234	
235	// Two windows per bucket rather than one: a short window stops a burst, and a
236	// long one stops a patient attacker who paces themselves just under it.
237	const LOGIN_IP_RULES: Rule[] = [
238	  { limit: 20, windowMs: 15 * MINUTE },
239	  { limit: 60, windowMs: HOUR },
240	];
241	
242	// Per ACCOUNT, across every source address. This is the rule that actually
243	// answers credential stuffing, where the whole point is that each guess arrives
244	// from a different IP. Tighter than the per-IP rule because a single account
245	// legitimately sees very few failures.
246	//
247	// The tradeoff is real and is chosen with eyes open: anyone can burn a victim's
248	// account bucket on purpose and cost them a login for a few minutes. That is
249	// why this is a ROLLING WINDOW that heals by itself, never a sticky lockout
250	// flag, and why a correct password clears it immediately — the victim's next
251	// attempt after the window slides succeeds, and no operator action is needed.
252	// An indefinite lockout would trade password guessing for a denial-of-service
253	// against any account whose email address is known.
254	const LOGIN_EMAIL_RULES: Rule[] = [
255	  { limit: 5, windowMs: 15 * MINUTE },
256	  { limit: 20, windowMs: HOUR },
257	];
258	
259	// Signup is a volume problem, not a guessing problem: one source minting many
260	// accounts. Every account that lands costs SIGNUP_GRANT credits of real model
261	// spend, so the daily rule is the one that bounds the money.
262	//
263	// Sized to be invisible to humans and to a shared office address (five accounts
264	// an hour from one IP is already an odd thing for real people to do) while
265	// capping what a single address can mint per day. A distributed botnet still
266	// gets one bucket per address — no IP-keyed limiter can fix that, and the
267	// answers to it are email verification before the grant lands, or deferring the
268	// grant until first build. Both are outside this file.
269	const SIGNUP_IP_RULES: Rule[] = [
270	  { limit: 5, windowMs: HOUR },
271	  { limit: 15, windowMs: DAY },
272	];
273	
274	const loginIp: Store = { scope: "ip", rules: LOGIN_IP_RULES, hits: new Map() };
275	const loginAccount: Store = { scope: "account", rules: LOGIN_EMAIL_RULES, hits: new Map() };
276	const signupIp: Store = { scope: "signup", rules: SIGNUP_IP_RULES, hits: new Map() };
277	const STORES: Store[] = [loginIp, loginAccount, signupIp];
278	const STORE_BY_SCOPE = new Map<string, Store>(STORES.map((s) => [s.scope, s]));
279	
280	// Ceiling on distinct keys per store, so a flood of unique addresses cannot
281	// grow memory without bound.
282	const MAX_KEYS = 20_000;
283	
284	function longestWindow(rules: Rule[]): number {
285	  return Math.max(...rules.map((r) => r.windowMs));
286	}
287	
288	function highestLimit(rules: Rule[]): number {
289	  return Math.max(...rules.map((r) => r.limit));
290	}
291	
292	/** The longest window any rule uses. Nothing older can affect any verdict. */
293	const MAX_WINDOW = Math.max(...STORES.map((s) => longestWindow(s.rules)));
294	
295	/**
296	 * Keep a store under MAX_KEYS.
297	 *
298	 * NOTE the difference from checkEnhanceRateLimit above, which clears wholesale
299	 * when it grows too large. That is fine for a speed bump on an authenticated
300	 * route; here it would be a vulnerability — an attacker could flood unique keys
301	 * to force a clear and wipe the very counter that is throttling them. So this
302	 * only ever drops entries that are already expired, and if that is not enough,
303	 * evicts the LEAST recently active first. An attacker's own bucket is by
304	 * definition the most recently active, so it is the last thing to go.
305	 *
306	 * Eviction is a memory decision only, never a durability one: the rows stay in
307	 * LoginAttempt, so an evicted key comes back at the next reconcile with its
308	 * count intact.
309	 */
310	function sweep(store: Store, now: number): void {
311	  if (store.hits.size <= MAX_KEYS) return;
312	  const windowMs = longestWindow(store.rules);
313	
314	  for (const [key, hits] of store.hits) {
315	    if (hits.length === 0 || hits[hits.length - 1].at <= now - windowMs) store.hits.delete(key);
316	  }
317	  if (store.hits.size <= MAX_KEYS) return;
318	
319	  const byLastSeen = [...store.hits.entries()].sort(
320	    (a, b) => a[1][a[1].length - 1].at - b[1][b[1].length - 1].at,
321	  );
322	  for (const [key] of byLastSeen.slice(0, store.hits.size - MAX_KEYS)) store.hits.delete(key);
323	}
324	
325	/** Read-only: would one more hit on this key breach any of its rules? */
326	function check(store: Store, key: string): Verdict {
327	  const now = Date.now();
328	  const rules = store.rules;
329	  const hits = (store.hits.get(key) ?? []).filter((h) => h.at > now - longestWindow(rules));
330	
331	  let retryAfterSeconds = 0;
332	  for (const rule of rules) {
333	    const inWindow = hits.filter((h) => h.at > now - rule.windowMs);
334	    if (inWindow.length < rule.limit) continue;
335	    // Wait only until enough hits age out of THIS window, not a flat period.
336	    const binding = inWindow[inWindow.length - rule.limit];
337	    retryAfterSeconds = Math.max(
338	      retryAfterSeconds,
339	      Math.max(1, Math.ceil((binding.at + rule.windowMs - now) / 1000)),
340	    );
341	  }
342	
343	  return retryAfterSeconds > 0 ? { allowed: false, retryAfterSeconds } : { allowed: true };
344	}

346	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
347	// Durable side: one serialised write queue, plus tombstones
348	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
349	
350	/**
351	 * Every mutation is queued here and never awaited by a request.
352	 *
353	 * SERIALISED, not merely fire-and-forget, and that ordering is load-bearing:
354	 * `refund` deletes the row that `record` inserts, and if the DELETE could
355	 * overtake the INSERT the row would survive and the refund would silently do
356	 * nothing. One chain guarantees the two run in call order. The chain never
357	 * rejects — a failed write is dropped, because the alternative (throwing into a
358	 * request that has already been answered) helps nobody, and the next reconcile
359	 * re-reads whatever actually landed.
360	 */
361	let writes: Promise<unknown> = Promise.resolve();
362	function enqueueWrite(run: () => Promise<unknown>): void {
363	  writes = writes.then(() => run().catch(() => undefined));
364	}
365	
366	/**
367	 * Rows we have deleted (or are about to) whose DELETE may not have committed
368	 * before an in-flight reconcile read them. Without this a refund could be
369	 * undone by a read that started a moment earlier. Id ⇒ expiry.
370	 */
371	const tombstones = new Map<string, number>();
372	/** Buckets cleared by a successful login. `scope\0key` ⇒ the moment of clearing. */
373	const cleared = new Map<string, number>();
374	const TOMBSTONE_MS = 60_000;
375	
376	function bucketId(scope: Scope, key: string): string {
377	  return `${scope}:${key}`;
378	}
379	
380	/**
381	 * Consume one hit: append to the index synchronously, queue the row.
382	 *
383	 * `createdAt` is set from this process's clock rather than left to the database
384	 * default, so that a row and the in-memory hit it mirrors carry the SAME
385	 * timestamp. `check` measures every window against `Date.now()`, and letting the
386	 * two clocks disagree would move hits across a window edge at each reconcile.
387	 */
388	function record(store: Store, key: string): void {
389	  const now = Date.now();
390	  sweep(store, now);
391	  const hits = (store.hits.get(key) ?? []).filter((h) => h.at > now - longestWindow(store.rules));
392	  const hit: Hit = { id: randomUUID(), at: now };
393	  hits.push(hit);
394	  store.hits.set(key, hits);
395	
396	  const scope = store.scope;
397	  enqueueWrite(async () => {
398	    await db.loginAttempt.create({ data: { id: hit.id, key, scope, createdAt: new Date(hit.at) } });
399	    hit.settledAt = Date.now();
400	  });
401	}
402	
403	/**
404	 * Give back the single most recent hit on a key.
405	 *
406	 * WHY A DELETE, AND NOT A COMPENSATING ROW. A row here is not a record that an
407	 * event occurred — LoginAttempt has no outcome column, nothing reads it but this
408	 * file, and nothing in the product or the admin surfaces it. It is one unit of
409	 * budget that has been spent. Handing the unit back therefore means removing the
410	 * row: the table is a counter, and the honest way to decrement a counter made of
411	 * rows is to delete one. A "negative" marker would mean the count query stops
412	 * being `count(*)` over an index range and becomes a signed sum, which is
413	 * strictly slower, and it would leave rows that outlive their own window and
414	 * still change a verdict. If this table ever needs to double as an audit log,
415	 * that is a different table with a different retention answer, not a sign bit
416	 * bolted onto this one.
417	 *
418	 * WHICH row: the newest for the key, which is what the in-memory predecessor did
419	 * (`hits.pop()`). It is not necessarily the row this very request inserted — a
420	 * concurrent attempt from the same IP may have landed in between — but the
421	 * effect on every window that contains both is identical, and picking the newest
422	 * is the conservative choice, since giving back an older hit would extend the
423	 * bucket's memory rather than shorten it.
424	 */
425	function refund(store: Store, key: string): void {
426	  const hits = store.hits.get(key);
427	  const hit = hits?.pop();
428	  if (!hits || !hit) return;
429	  if (hits.length === 0) store.hits.delete(key);
430	
431	  tombstones.set(hit.id, Date.now() + TOMBSTONE_MS);
432	  enqueueWrite(() => db.loginAttempt.deleteMany({ where: { id: hit.id } }));
433	}
434	
435	/**
436	 * Empty a bucket outright: the account half of a successful login.
437	 *
438	 * Deletes by `(scope, key)` rather than by the ids this process happens to know,
439	 * so guesses recorded against the same account by another process — or before a
440	 * restart — go too. Bounded to rows that existed at the moment of success, so a
441	 * guess arriving during the delete is still counted.
442	 */
443	function clearBucket(store: Store, key: string): void {
444	  const at = Date.now();
445	  store.hits.delete(key);
446	  cleared.set(bucketId(store.scope, key), at);
447	
448	  const scope = store.scope;
449	  enqueueWrite(() =>
450	    db.loginAttempt.deleteMany({ where: { scope, key, createdAt: { lte: new Date(at) } } }),
451	  );
452	}

454	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
455	// Reconcile: rebuild the in-process index from LoginAttempt
456	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
457	
458	const RECONCILE_MS = 10_000;
459	
460	/**
461	 * How often the SIGNUP scope is re-read, as opposed to the two login scopes.
462	 *
463	 * The login scopes need an hour of history and the signup scope needs a day, and
464	 * that difference is the whole cost of a reconcile. An hour's rows are a bounded
465	 * backward walk of LoginAttempt_createdAt_idx that stops at the window edge
466	 * (measured: 1305 rows, 24 buffers, 0.3ms against a 30k-row table). A day's
467	 * signup rows are most of the signup rows there are — the prune keeps barely
468	 * more than a day — so once the table is large enough Postgres will and should
469	 * stop using an index for them and read the table instead (measured: 3.5ms).
470	 * There is no index that makes "most of a column's rows" cheap, so the answer is
471	 * to ask less often rather than to ask differently. Signup is the slow-moving
472	 * bucket — five an hour per address — and a minute of divergence between two
473	 * processes is nothing against a daily cap of fifteen.
474	 */
475	const FULL_RECONCILE_MS = 60_000;
476	
477	/**
478	 * Cap on rows pulled per query. A guard against a pathological table, not an
479	 * expected case: the prune keeps at most a day of rows, and the limits cap what
480	 * one key can contribute. If it ever binds, `truncated` below degrades the
481	 * limiter to its old in-memory behaviour rather than to no limiter at all.
482	 */
483	const MAX_RECONCILE_ROWS = 20_000;
484	
485	/**
486	 * Rebuild the index from the table.
487	 *
488	 * `allScopes` false rebuilds only the two login scopes, which is the common
489	 * tick; the signup scope is left exactly as it is. See FULL_RECONCILE_MS.
490	 */
491	async function reconcile(allScopes: boolean): Promise<void> {
492	  const startedAt = Date.now();
493	  const stores = allScopes ? STORES : STORES.filter((s) => s.scope !== "signup");
494	
495	  // TWO queries rather than one over the longest window, because the two halves
496	  // want different windows and different plans:
497	  //  * an hour covers both login scopes, and `createdAt > $cutoff ORDER BY
498	  //    "createdAt" DESC` is a backward scan of LoginAttempt_createdAt_idx that
499	  //    stops at the window edge — its cost is the rows it returns, nothing more;
500	  //  * a day of signup rows is fetched separately, so the cheap query is not
501	  //    dragged out to 24× its width by a scope that changes far more slowly.
502	  // The hour of signup rows the first query also returns is deduplicated by id.
503	  const columns = { id: true, scope: true, key: true, createdAt: true } as const;
504	  const [recent, signups] = await Promise.all([
505	    db.loginAttempt.findMany({
506	      where: { createdAt: { gt: new Date(startedAt - HOUR) } },
507	      select: columns,
508	      orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" },
509	      take: MAX_RECONCILE_ROWS,
510	    }),
511	    allScopes
512	      ? db.loginAttempt.findMany({
513	          where: { scope: "signup", createdAt: { gt: new Date(startedAt - DAY) } },
514	          select: columns,
515	          orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" },
516	          take: MAX_RECONCILE_ROWS,
517	        })
518	      : [],
519	  ]);
520	  const truncated = recent.length >= MAX_RECONCILE_ROWS || signups.length >= MAX_RECONCILE_ROWS;
521	
522	  const next = new Map<Scope, Map<string, Hit[]>>(stores.map((s) => [s.scope, new Map()]));
523	  const seen = new Set<string>();
524	
525	  // Rows arrive newest-first, so a bucket that has already collected its rule
526	  // ceiling can stop: the ones left are older and cannot change any verdict.
527	  for (const row of [...recent, ...signups]) {
528	    if (seen.has(row.id)) continue;
529	    seen.add(row.id);
530	
531	    const store = STORE_BY_SCOPE.get(row.scope);
532	    const bucket = store && next.get(store.scope);
533	    if (!store || !bucket) continue;
534	
535	    const at = row.createdAt.getTime();
536	    if (at <= startedAt - longestWindow(store.rules)) continue;
537	    if (tombstones.has(row.id)) continue;
538	    const clearedAt = cleared.get(bucketId(store.scope, row.key));
539	    if (clearedAt !== undefined && at <= clearedAt) continue;
540	
541	    const arr = bucket.get(row.key) ?? [];
542	    if (arr.length >= highestLimit(store.rules)) continue;
543	    arr.push({ id: row.id, at, settledAt: at });
544	    bucket.set(row.key, arr);
545	  }
546	
547	  // Union with what this process holds that the read could not have seen: hits
548	  // recorded while the queries were in flight, and hits whose INSERT has not
549	  // committed yet. Read here, at apply time, so a refund or a clear that
550	  // happened during the queries is already reflected.
551	  //
552	  // The test is `settledAt`, not "recorded recently". The difference matters as
553	  // soon as there is more than one process: a hit of ours that we KNOW was
554	  // committed before the read began, and that the read did not return, is a row
555	  // another process has refunded or cleared. Re-adding it on a timer would
556	  // resurrect somebody else's refund for the length of that timer. A hit whose
557	  // INSERT has not resolved, on the other hand, is genuinely invisible to the
558	  // read and must be carried over, or a burst would lose everything it recorded
559	  // while a reconcile was in flight.
560	  for (const store of stores) {
561	    const bucket = next.get(store.scope);
562	    if (!bucket) continue;
563	    const windowMs = longestWindow(store.rules);
564	
565	    for (const [key, hits] of store.hits) {
566	      for (const hit of hits) {
567	        if (seen.has(hit.id) || tombstones.has(hit.id)) continue;
568	        if (hit.at <= startedAt - windowMs) continue;
569	        if (!truncated && hit.settledAt !== undefined && hit.settledAt <= startedAt) continue;
570	        const arr = bucket.get(key) ?? [];
571	        arr.push(hit);
572	        bucket.set(key, arr);
573	      }
574	    }
575	  }
576	
577	  const now = Date.now();
578	  for (const store of stores) {
579	    const bucket = next.get(store.scope);
580	    if (!bucket) continue;
581	    // `check` reads oldest-first.
582	    for (const hits of bucket.values()) hits.sort((a, b) => a.at - b.at);
583	    store.hits = bucket;
584	    sweep(store, now);
585	  }
586	
587	  for (const [id, expiry] of tombstones) if (expiry <= now) tombstones.delete(id);
588	  for (const [id, at] of cleared) if (at + TOMBSTONE_MS <= now) cleared.delete(id);
589	}

591	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
592	// Prune
593	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
594	
595	// WHY HERE AND NOT IN lib/retention.ts. Two reasons, one of them decisive.
596	//
597	// The decisive one: this file is the only one in scope, so adding a fifth rule
598	// to the retention policy is not mine to do. Someone who wants it there should
599	// read the second reason first, because I do not think it belongs there.
600	//
601	// A retention rule answers "how long should we keep data that still means
602	// something", and every rule in that file is a judgement call with a reader
603	// behind it — sessions, snapshots, analytics, Stripe idempotency. A LoginAttempt
604	// older than MAX_WINDOW means nothing to anybody: no query can reach it, no
605	// verdict can be changed by it, no product surface reads this table at all. It
606	// is not retained data, it is spent counter state, and collecting it is part of
607	// operating the counter rather than a policy anyone should have to weigh in on.
608	// Putting it in the policy file would also make correctness depend on a cron
609	// entry that (per that file's own header) nothing runs yet — the table would
610	// grow unbounded until someone wired up a job, which is a poor property for a
611	// table on the login path.
612	//
613	// So it runs here, on the reconcile timer rather than on the request path: an
614	// attacker's traffic must never be able to trigger extra DB work, and a delete
615	// on a request would do exactly that. Batched, with a ceiling per pass, for the
616	// same reason lib/retention.ts batches — no statement holds locks long enough
617	// to be noticed by someone signing in.
618	const PRUNE_EVERY_MS = 10 * MINUTE;
619	const PRUNE_BATCH = 500;
620	const PRUNE_MAX_BATCHES = 40;
621	/** Slack past MAX_WINDOW. A row at the edge is already unreadable; this just
622	 *  keeps the prune from racing the window it is trailing. */
623	const PRUNE_GRACE_MS = HOUR;
624	
625	let lastPruneAt = 0;
626	
627	// Select-then-delete rather than one `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ...)`, for
628	// the same reason lib/retention.ts is shaped this way — and for one more.
629	// LoginAttempt.createdAt is `timestamp(3)` WITHOUT a time zone, and a JS Date
630	// interpolated into $executeRaw is bound as `timestamptz`, so Postgres converts
631	// it using the session's TimeZone before comparing. On a server that is not on
632	// UTC that silently moves the cutoff by the local offset — measured here as
633	// seven hours, which would have pruned rows that were still inside their own
634	// window. The Prisma query builder knows the column's type and binds correctly.
635	async function prune(): Promise<void> {
636	  const cutoff = new Date(Date.now() - MAX_WINDOW - PRUNE_GRACE_MS);
637	  for (let i = 0; i < PRUNE_MAX_BATCHES; i++) {
638	    // An ordered range scan of LoginAttempt_createdAt_idx with a LIMIT, then a
639	    // delete by primary key.
640	    const stale = await db.loginAttempt.findMany({
641	      where: { createdAt: { lt: cutoff } },
642	      select: { id: true },
643	      orderBy: { createdAt: "asc" },
644	      take: PRUNE_BATCH,
645	    });
646	    if (stale.length === 0) return;
647	    await db.loginAttempt.deleteMany({ where: { id: { in: stale.map((r) => r.id) } } });
648	    if (stale.length < PRUNE_BATCH) return;
649	  }
650	}

652	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
653	// Lifecycle
654	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
655	
656	/** False until the index has been built from the table at least once. */
657	let hydrated = false;
658	let started = false;
659	let cycle: Promise<void> | null = null;
660	let lastFullAt = 0;
661	
662	function runCycle(force = false): Promise<void> {
663	  if (cycle) return cycle;
664	  cycle = (async () => {
665	    try {
666	      // A process's first cycle is always a full one: there is nothing in memory
667	      // yet for a partial one to leave alone.
668	      const allScopes = force || !hydrated || Date.now() - lastFullAt >= FULL_RECONCILE_MS;
669	      await reconcile(allScopes);
670	      if (allScopes) lastFullAt = Date.now();
671	      hydrated = true;
672	      if (Date.now() - lastPruneAt >= PRUNE_EVERY_MS) {
673	        lastPruneAt = Date.now();
674	        await prune();
675	      }
676	    } catch {
677	      // The database is unreachable. Both auth routes are broken anyway; stay
678	      // closed if we never hydrated, and keep serving the last known index if
679	      // we did. Retried on the next tick either way.
680	    } finally {
681	      cycle = null;
682	    }
683	  })();
684	  return cycle;
685	}

687	/**
688	 * Started by the first gate call rather than at import time, deliberately: a
689	 * module-level query would run during `next build`, which imports route modules
690	 * and has no business needing a database.
691	 */
692	function ensureStarted(): void {
693	  if (started) return;
694	  started = true;
695	  void runCycle();
696	  const timer = setInterval(() => void runCycle(), RECONCILE_MS) as unknown as {
697	    unref?: () => void;
698	  };
699	  // Never hold the process open for a counter refresh.
700	  timer.unref?.();
701	}

703	/** The verdict before the index exists. See COLD START above. */
704	function cold(): Verdict {
705	  return { allowed: false, retryAfterSeconds: 1 };

708	/**
709	 * Flush queued writes and rebuild the index from the table, immediately.
710	 *
711	 * Nothing on the request path needs this — the timer does it — but it is what
712	 * makes the durable behaviour testable without waiting on wall-clock intervals,
713	 * and it is the hook to call from a script that has just changed LoginAttempt
714	 * out from under a running process. It is additive: no existing signature moved,
715	 * so neither auth route changes.
716	 */
717	export async function syncLoginAttempts(): Promise<void> {
718	  ensureStarted();
719	  // Twice: a cycle already in flight may have read the table before the writes
720	  // being flushed here committed, so the first pass only guarantees that cycle
721	  // is over. The second is guaranteed to start after them.
722	  await writes;
723	  await runCycle(true);
724	  await writes;
725	  await runCycle(true);
726	}
727	
728	/**
729	 * Gate one sign-in attempt. Call BEFORE looking the user up or hashing
730	 * anything, and treat `allowed: false` as the end of the request.
731	 *
732	 * WHY THIS CONSUMES ON EVERY ATTEMPT RATHER THAN COUNTING FAILURES: counting
733	 * only failures means the counter is written after `verifyPassword` resolves,
734	 * and everything between is an `await`. A thousand concurrent guesses would all
735	 * pass the check before the first failure was ever recorded — the limiter would
736	 * read as correct and stop nothing. Consuming up front closes that window,
737	 * because the check and the record here happen in one synchronous run with no
738	 * await between them. It is also why the durable counter is read from an index
739	 * in memory rather than queried: a `SELECT count(*)` would put an await back in
740	 * the middle of the gate and reopen the hole this closes. A correct password is
741	 * then refunded by noteLoginSuccess, which gets back the failure-counting
742	 * behaviour without the race.
743	 *
744	 * The verdict is identical whether or not `email` belongs to a real account —
745	 * the account bucket fills on attempts, not on hits — so a 429 tells an
746	 * enumerating caller nothing that a 401 would not.
747	 */
748	export function checkLoginRateLimit(req: Request, email: string): Verdict {
749	  ensureStarted();
750	  if (!hydrated) return cold();
751	
752	  const ip = clientIp(req);
753	  const account = emailKey(email);
754	
755	  // Both verdicts are taken before either is consumed. Otherwise an attacker
756	  // already blocked on their own IP would keep filling victims' account buckets
757	  // — turning a limiter into a lockout tool.
758	  const byIp = check(loginIp, ip);
759	  const byAccount = check(loginAccount, account);
760	  if (!byIp.allowed || !byAccount.allowed) {
761	    return {
762	      allowed: false,
763	      retryAfterSeconds: Math.max(byIp.retryAfterSeconds ?? 0, byAccount.retryAfterSeconds ?? 0),
764	    };
765	  }
766	
767	  record(loginIp, ip);
768	  record(loginAccount, account);
769	  return { allowed: true };
770	}
771	
772	/**
773	 * Call after a password verifies. Clears the account's bucket outright, and
774	 * refunds this attempt against the IP's.
775	 *
776	 * The two are treated differently on purpose. Clearing the account bucket is
777	 * safe: whoever just proved they hold the password is entitled to that account.
778	 * The IP bucket is only REFUNDED — one hit, the successful one — so that a NAT
779	 * shared by hundreds of people is never spent by people signing in correctly,
780	 * while an attacker who happens to own one valid account cannot log into it
781	 * repeatedly to wipe the guesses they are making against everyone else.
782	 */
783	export function noteLoginSuccess(req: Request, email: string): void {
784	  ensureStarted();
785	  clearBucket(loginAccount, emailKey(email));
786	  refund(loginIp, clientIp(req));
787	}
788	
789	/**
790	 * Gate one signup attempt. Call once the request is well-formed and BEFORE the
791	 * existence check, so that hammering signup to learn which emails are already
792	 * registered is throttled by the same counter as account minting.
793	 *
794	 * Consumes on every attempt, with no refund for success — unlike login, a
795	 * successful signup is precisely the expensive event we are limiting.
796	 */
797	export function checkSignupRateLimit(req: Request): Verdict {
798	  ensureStarted();
799	  if (!hydrated) return cold();
800	
801	  const ip = clientIp(req);
802	  const verdict = check(signupIp, ip);
803	  if (!verdict.allowed) return verdict;
804	  record(signupIp, ip);
805	  return { allowed: true };
806	}
807	
808	/**
809	 * The one message either auth route shows when it throttles. Uniform by
810	 * design: it must not differ between the per-IP and the per-account rule, or
811	 * between a registered address and an unregistered one, because the difference
812	 * would itself be the answer to "does this account exist".
813	 */
814	export const RATE_LIMITED_MESSAGE = "Too many attempts. Please wait a moment and try again.";

7	// ── Account-level data export (an access request, self-served) ────────────
8	//
9	// NOT to be confused with app/api/projects/[id]/export/route.ts, which zips ONE
10	// project's draft source tree. This is the account-level answer the privacy
11	// policy points at: everything the product database holds about the person
12	// making the request, in one JSON document they can read without us.
13	//
14	// Three rules shape it:
15	//
16	// 1. SCOPED BY THE REQUESTER'S ID IN THE SAME QUERY AS ANY OTHER ID. Every
17	//    query below carries `userId` (or `project: { userId }`) in its own WHERE,
18	//    never "look up the project, then trust the id". Same rule the project
19	//    routes follow, for the same reason: another user's row must be
20	//    indistinguishable from a row that does not exist.
21	// 2. STREAMED, NOT BUFFERED. A single Response.json() would hold the entire
22	//    account — every file, every build snapshot — in memory as objects AND
23	//    again as a string. Build snapshots are full copies of a file tree per
24	//    successful build, so a heavy account is tens of megabytes. This assembles
25	//    the document in pages, the way lib/zip.ts streams an archive.
26	// 3. WHAT IS LEFT OUT IS NAMED IN THE FILE ITSELF. An export that silently
27	//    omits things is worse than one that says what it omits and why — see
28	//    NOT_INCLUDED below, which ships inside the download.
29	
30	const FORMAT = "kodely.account-export";
31	const FORMAT_VERSION = 1;
32	
33	/** Rows per page for most tables. */
34	const PAGE = 200;
35	
36	/**
37	 * Builds are paged far smaller because each one can carry `filesSnapshot` — a
38	 * whole file tree. 200 of those at once would defeat the point of streaming.
39	 */
40	const BUILD_PAGE = 20;
41	
42	/**
43	 * One export per user per minute.
44	 *
45	 * A full account dump is the most expensive read in the product, and nothing
46	 * else here is rate limited by user id at this cost. In memory and
47	 * per-process, exactly like checkEnhanceRateLimit in lib/rate-limit.ts, and
48	 * with the same honest limitation: it resets on deploy and multiplies if the
49	 * app is ever run as more than one process. That is adequate for a speed bump
50	 * on an authenticated route — this is not a security control, it is a guard
51	 * against a stuck client re-downloading in a loop.
52	 */
53	const COOLDOWN_MS = 60_000;
54	const MAX_KEYS = 5_000;
55	const lastExportAt = new Map<string, number>();
56	
57	function throttled(userId: string): number | null {
58	  const now = Date.now();
59	  const previous = lastExportAt.get(userId);
60	  if (previous !== undefined && now - previous < COOLDOWN_MS) {
61	    return Math.ceil((COOLDOWN_MS - (now - previous)) / 1000);
62	  }
63	  // Bounded so a long-lived process cannot accumulate one entry per user
64	  // forever. Clearing wholesale only ever grants an extra export.
65	  if (lastExportAt.size > MAX_KEYS) lastExportAt.clear();
66	  lastExportAt.set(userId, now);
67	  return null;
68	}
69	
70	/**
71	 * Stated inside the download. Everything here is either not held in the
72	 * product database at all, or is somebody else's personal data.
73	 */
74	const NOT_INCLUDED: { item: string; why: string }[] = [
75	  {
76	    item: "Your password",
77	    why: "Stored only as a salted scrypt hash, which is not reversible and is of no use to you.",
78	  },
79	  {
80	    item: "Session tokens",
81	    why: "Only a SHA-256 hash of each token is stored. The sessions themselves are listed below without it.",
82	  },
83	  {
84	    item: "The staff email address on each support note",
85	    why: "That is another person's contact detail. The note's text and date are included in full.",
86	  },
87	  {
88	    item: "Admin audit-log entries",
89	    why: "They record which operator performed an action, so they identify staff rather than you, and they are a security log.",
90	  },
91	  {
92	    item: "Web server and CDN access logs",
93	    why: "IP addresses and timestamps recorded by the servers in front of the app. They live outside the product database and are not queryable per account.",
94	  },
95	  {
96	    item: "Pre-authentication rate-limit counters",
97	    why: "Keyed by a salted hash of an IP address or email address specifically so they cannot be matched back to an account.",
98	  },
99	  {
100	    item: "Contact-form messages",
101	    why: "Emailed to our inbox and never written to the product database.",
102	  },
103	  {
104	    item: "Data held by Anthropic, Stripe, Google or Discord",
105	    why: "Those companies hold their own records under their own policies. Ask them directly.",
106	  },

109	/**
110	 * Emit a JSON array without ever holding the whole thing in memory.
111	 *
112	 * `page` is re-invoked with a growing offset until it returns a short page.
113	 * Offset paging can in principle skip or repeat a row if the table is written
114	 * to mid-export; every ordering below is `createdAt asc, id asc` over rows
115	 * that only the requesting user creates, so the practical exposure is one
116	 * project they created in the seconds the download took.
117	 */
118	async function* jsonArray<T>(
119	  page: (skip: number, take: number) => Promise<T[]>,
120	  shape: (row: T) => unknown,
121	  size = PAGE,
122	): AsyncGenerator<string> {
123	  yield "[";
124	  let skip = 0;
125	  let first = true;
126	  for (;;) {
127	    const rows = await page(skip, size);
128	    for (const row of rows) {
129	      yield (first ? "" : ",") + JSON.stringify(shape(row));
130	      first = false;
131	    }
132	    if (rows.length < size) break;
133	    skip += rows.length;
134	  }
135	  yield "]";
136	}

138	/**
139	 * `reward:<platform>:<hash>` (granted) or `reward:<platform>:pending:<hash>`
140	 * (declared, still on hold). The format is owned by app/api/rewards/_lib.ts —
141	 * parsed structurally here rather than importing that module's helpers, so the
142	 * export needs no knowledge of which platforms exist or what a hash means.
143	 */
144	function rewardFromReason(
145	  reason: string,
146	): { platform: string; pending: boolean; identityHash: string } | null {
147	  const parts = reason.split(":");
148	  if (parts[0] !== "reward" || parts.length < 3) return null;
149	  const pending = parts[2] === "pending";
150	  const identityHash = pending ? parts[3] : parts[2];
151	  if (!identityHash) return null;
152	  return { platform: parts[1], pending, identityHash };

403	  yield* jsonArray(

419	  // list is short-circuited rather than becoming `IN ()`.

427	            where: { projectId: { in: projectIds } },
428	            orderBy: [{ createdAt: "asc" }, { id: "asc" }],
429	            select: {
430	              projectId: true,
431	              rule: true,
432	              severity: true,
433	              path: true,
434	              evidence: true,
435	              action: true,
436	              createdAt: true,
437	              reviewedAt: true,

449	export async function GET() {
450	  const user = await requireUser().catch(() => null);
451	  if (!user) return Response.json({ error: "Not signed in." }, { status: 401 });
452	
453	  const retryAfter = throttled(user.id);
454	  if (retryAfter !== null) {
455	    return Response.json(
456	      { error: "An export was just generated. Try again in a moment." },
457	      { status: 429, headers: { "Retry-After": String(retryAfter) } },
458	    );
459	  }
460	
461	  const chunks = exportChunks({ id: user.id });
462	  const encoder = new TextEncoder();
463	
464	  const stream = new ReadableStream<Uint8Array>({
465	    async pull(controller) {
466	      // A query that throws mid-document errors the stream, which the browser
467	      // surfaces as a failed download rather than a truncated file. The status
468	      // line has already been sent by then, so there is no way to turn it into
469	      // a 500 — failing the transfer is the honest alternative.
470	      const { done, value } = await chunks.next();
471	      if (done) controller.close();
472	      else controller.enqueue(encoder.encode(value));
473	    },
474	    cancel() {
475	      void chunks.return(undefined);
476	    },
477	  });
478	
479	  const stamp = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);
480	
481	  return new Response(stream, {
482	    headers: {
483	      "Content-Type": "application/json; charset=utf-8",
484	      "Content-Disposition": `attachment; filename="kodely-account-export-${stamp}.json"`,
485	      "Cache-Control": "no-store",
486	    },
487	  });
488	}

/**
 * The other half of the policy: what is deliberately kept forever, and why.
 * A retention document that lists only deletions is not a policy, it is a
 * changelog — these are the commitments someone can be held to.
 */
export const NEVER_PRUNED: { target: string; reason: string }[] = [
  {
    target: "CreditLedger",
    reason:
      "An auditable financial record. The balance is derived from the ledger rather than " +
      "stored as a counter (lib/credits.ts, and the DISTINCT ON balance query in " +
      "app/admin/users/page.tsx), so removing any row rewrites history and can change a " +
      "live balance. It survives project deletion by design — buildId goes null, the row " +
      "stays. Retained permanently.",
  },
  {
    target: "Build (the row, as opposed to its snapshot)",
    reason:
      "Two unbounded readers make deletion unsafe: app/admin/page.tsx and " +
      "app/admin/users/[id]/page.tsx both run db.build.aggregate over ALL builds for " +
      "lifetime costMicros and creditsCharged, and CreditLedger.buildId points here " +
      "(ON DELETE SET NULL), so deleting builds silently detaches spend from what caused " +
      "it. Kept for the life of the project; deleting a project cascades them away.",
  },
  {
    target: "Build.prompt",
    reason:
      "Free text the user wrote, so a tempting redaction target — but it is the visible " +
      "label of every checkpoint in the history panel " +
      "(app/api/projects/[id]/builds/route.ts selects it). Redacting old prompts would " +
      "turn old checkpoints into unlabelled rows. Kept for the life of the project.",
  },
  {
    target: "ProjectFile / Message / Project",
    reason:
      "The user's actual work and conversation. These are the product, not exhaust. They " +
      "are deleted when the user deletes the project or their account, and never on a " +
      "timer.",
  },
  {
    target: "EmailLog",
    reason:
      "The idempotency guard for transactional email, and the one table here where a " +
      "delete can produce a WRONG ACTION rather than a missing statistic: the row IS the " +
      "claim (the unique (kind, dedupeKey) is what makes a send exactly-once), so removing " +
      "one re-arms that send. dedupeKey is the id of the thing that triggered the mail — a " +
      "ledger row, a build, a project — never a timestamp, so a claim does not expire and " +
      "there is no age at which it is safe to drop. The concrete path is site_published, " +
      "whose key is a projectId: a republish is only held back by a lifetime count of " +
      "project.published events (lib/notifications/scan.ts), which the 400-day event rule " +
      "eventually removes, leaving this row as the last thing standing between a republish " +
      "and a second email. It is also a reader-facing record — app/api/account/export " +
      "returns it as \"emailsSent\" in a person's own data export — and it is tiny (four " +
      "kinds, one short row each). NOTE: nothing writes this table today; " +
      "lib/notifications/send.ts dedupes in a process-local Map that resets on deploy. The " +
      "durable guard is declared and unwired, which makes this the wrong moment to also " +
      "put it on a timer. Deleted per person, not per clock: erasure removes a user's rows " +
      "(app/api/account/_deletion.ts).",
  },
  {
    target: "AdminAuditLog (rows whose action is a WRITE)",
    reason:
      "The accountability half of the log. An unrecorded write means state changed and " +
      "nothing anywhere says who changed it — and for one action the log is not a record " +
      "of the change, it is the ONLY record: takedown is not a column, so " +
      "app/admin/sites/page.tsx reconstructs which sites were taken down by grouping " +
      "site.taken_down rows. Pruning them would un-take-down sites in the registry view. " +
      "They are rare and small; the volume in this table is entirely on the read side, " +
      "which ages out at 180 days. Classified by `kind` in ADMIN_ACTION_INFO, so a new " +
      "write action is protected the moment it is declared, and any action name not in " +
      "that vocabulary is left alone.",
  },
  {
    target: "ModerationFinding (rows with reviewedAt = NULL)",
    reason:
      "An open work queue, not a record. app/admin/sites/page.tsx counts unreviewed " +
      "findings and lists the projects they point at; the takedown page gates on the same " +
      "count. Ageing one out would mean discarding an abuse report BEFORE anybody read it " +
      "and removing the flag that says the site needs looking at — a retention job " +
      "silently emptying a review queue is the worst failure available in this file. The " +
      "growth this leaves unbounded is bounded by doing the reviews; once reviewed, the " +
      "400-day rule takes them.",
  },
];

Now I'm designing the SupportTicket schema with fields for status, read-state tracking on both customer and staff sides, and timestamps for last message and closure.

For read tracking I'm weighing per-message readAt versus per-ticket lastReadAt timestamps for each side; a thread model favors two timestamps on the ticket itself—customerReadAt and staffReadAt—since that's simpler and more honest than tracking read state message-by-message. I'm also noting a tension around denormalizing the customer's email onto messages for staff visibility, since that could leave PII behind after account erasure even though the ticket cascades on user deletion.

For "unanswered," I decide status is the cleaner signal than comparing timestamps, so I'm defining a small three-value status vocabulary: OPEN (customer spoke last, system-set), ANSWERED (staff replied, system-set), and RESOLVED (closed by either party, human-set).

I still need read-state tracking on both sides since status only tells whose turn it is, not whether they've actually seen the latest message — so I'll keep customerReadAt, staffReadAt, and a lastMessageAt for ordering, though I need to be careful that a customer's own reply doesn't mistakenly mark their side as unread.

I'm settling on keeping all three timestamps updated within the same transaction as message writes, since `lastMessageAt` still needs to exist separately for ordering—Prisma can't do a GREATEST comparison in orderBy, so I can't just compute it from the other two fields in JS. Three columns, each with a distinct purpose, feels justified.

Actually, `lastMessageAt` is clearer for readers than relying on `updatedAt`. I'm reconsidering whether I really need three separate timestamp fields, but having both staff and customer variants alongside a general one feels redundant.

• Every project — name, URL slug, dates, whether it is live, and every file in it. Both the source tree you edit and the compiled output, in both their draft and published states. The per-project zip in the editor only ever contains draft source, so this is the complete version.
  • Every chat message in every project, yours and Kodely's.
  • Every build — the prompt, the model, token counts, the real cost in micro-dollars, credits charged, repair attempts, any error, and the full file snapshot taken after each successful build.
  • Your credit ledger — every grant and charge, with its reason and the balance it produced.
  • Your reward connections — which platforms you connected for free credits and when. What we store per connection is a keyed hash, not your username or account id, and the file explains that rather than presenting the hash as if it meant something.
  • Your analytics events — the first-party product events recorded against your user id, with their properties.
  • Operator notes written about you by our support staff, in full.
  • Sign-in sessions (when, and until when — never the token),{" "} transactional emails sent to you, and any{" "} publish-time moderation findings on your projects.

    • The file also carries a list of what is deliberately not in it and why — your password hash, session tokens, the staff email on each support note, admin audit records, server and CDN access logs, and data held by Anthropic, Stripe, Google or Discord under their own policies.

    What deletion destroys

    Deleting your account is irreversible. There is no soft-delete, no undo, and no backup a support agent can restore from. It destroys:

    • every project, and with it every file, every chat message and every build record, including the file snapshots that make rollback possible;
    • your published sites. Each one goes offline and its{" "} *.kodely.site address stops resolving. A page already cached at the CDN or in a visitor's browser can survive for up to a minute after that;
    • your email address, your name, your password hash, your linked Google account and your Stripe customer identifier;
    • every sign-in session, so you are signed out everywhere immediately;
    • every operator note written about you, and the record of transactional emails we sent you.

    Your credit balance goes with the account. Deleting is not a refund.

The category field defaults to "help" on the model, and the topic query param maps to these categories through a closed, hardened lookup table that also determines whether the ticket body gets a scaffold (bug reports get a prompt for expected/actual behavior and site info, feature requests don't), and the composer should auto-expand whenever a valid topic is passed in. Working through this, I settle on four columns: `lastMessageAt`, `lastStaffMessageAt`, `customerReadAt`, `staffReadAt`. Customer unread is derived from comparing `lastStaffMessageAt` to `customerReadAt`, while staff unread aligns naturally with the ticket being OPEN, since an open status implies the last message came from the customer, making `lastMessageAt` the relevant comparison point against `staffReadAt`.

content.content:
What we collect

Account information

Your email address, and either a password (stored as a salted scrypt hash — we never see or store your plaintext password) or, if you sign in with Google, your name and your Google account identifier. If you set a monthly spending cap, we store that number. If you buy credits, we store the customer identifier our payment processor gives us.

Project content

The project names and URL slugs you choose, the prompts you write, Kodely's replies, the source files it generates, and the compiled output of each build. This is the substance of the product: it is stored so your projects persist and can be edited, previewed, published and rolled back. If you attach a reference image to a prompt, it is sent to the model for that build but is not saved to your project.

A prompt you type on the homepage before you have an account stays in your own browser until you sign in and a project is created for it.

Build records

For every generation we record the prompt, which model ran, token counts, the computed cost, the credits charged, how many repair attempts the build needed, any error message, and — after a successful build — a full snapshot of your project's files at that moment. The snapshot is what makes rolling a project back to an earlier build possible.

Credits ledger

Every credit grant and charge, with the reason, the related build, and the resulting balance. The ledger is append-only, because a balance you can't audit is a balance you can't trust.

Product analytics

We keep a first-party event stream on our own infrastructure — no third-party analytics service is involved. Each record is an event name, your user id, a timestamp, and a small set of properties. The events we record today are: sign-up (and whether it was by password or Google), project created, project deleted, build started, build succeeded, build failed, build rated, site published, credits exhausted, self-imposed spending cap reached, checkout started, and credits purchased.

Technical data

Requests to kodely.me pass through a CDN and web servers that keep standard access logs, which include IP addresses and timestamps. Our contact form holds the sender IP in memory for up to an hour purely to rate-limit spam; it is not written to the database.

If you email us through the contact form

The name, email address and message you submit are emailed to our own inbox so we can reply. They are not stored in the product database.

How we use it

To operate your account and projects; to generate, compile and repair the sites you ask for; to meter credits accurately and honour the spending cap you set; to keep the service and the sites we host secure and free of abuse; to understand where the product is failing people, using the

How long we keep it

We want to be straightforward here rather than quote a number nothing enforces. Kodely does not run any automatic deletion job. In practice:

  • Projects, files, chat messages and build records are kept until you delete the project. Deleting a project removes its files, messages and builds — including the file snapshots — and takes any published site offline. A cached copy of a published page can survive at the CDN or in a visitor's browser for up to a minute after that.
  • Credit ledger entries survive project deletion, with the reference to the deleted build cleared. Deleting work does not un-charge the credits it used, and an auditable balance depends on those rows staying put.
  • Analytics events are retained indefinitely today. They are not deleted when a project is deleted. If your account is deleted, the events remain but are detached from you — the user id on them is cleared.
  • Sessions expire 30 days after sign-in, and are removed when you sign out.
  • Account data is kept for as long as your account exists. When you delete your account, your email address, name, password hash and linked accounts are destroyed along with your projects; the credit ledger and the moderation record of any blocked publish survive, no longer linked to your name or your email address. Exactly what goes and what stays is itemised on{" "} Your data and your rights.

Your choices and your rights
